Something Is Cooking in America. Coincidence or a Bigger Story?

Something unusual is happening in the United States. Within a few days, several major technology companies, government agencies and critical services have faced unexpected disruptions.

Microsoft experienced a global outage affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot. The FAA faced air traffic control communication problems, while the NSA reported an issue with its internal communications network. Amazon Web Services (AWS), Workday and Anthropic's Claude also experienced service disruptions.

The list does not end there. JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America faced banking service issues, United Airlines experienced flight disruptions, and Apple and Marriott also reported technical problems.

These incidents have been attributed to different causes, including software bugs, system updates, maintenance and infrastructure failures. There is no confirmed evidence connecting them to a single coordinated event.

But the timing is certainly raising questions.

Are these just unrelated technical failures, or are we witnessing something bigger involving America's digital infrastructure, cybersecurity and national security systems?

Perhaps it is a series of coincidences. Or perhaps there is a bigger story unfolding behind the scenes.

Something is cooking. The real question is: what?🤔
#conspiracy

Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue this week, up 103% from a year ago. In the same week, fund managers cut their tech exposure at the fastest pace since 2006.

Both signals are real. Here is what they tell us.

The numbers:

→ Nvidia's Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110%
→ Fourth-quarter revenue is guided to $130 billion, excluding any China Data Center compute revenue
→ Tech overweight among fund managers fell from 37% to 12% in a month (Bank of America survey)
→ A record net 38% say companies are overinvesting in AI
→ 52% expect a hyperscaler to cut capital spending within six months

Why they do not contradict each other: Nvidia is a supplier, so its revenue reflects spending customers have already committed. Investors are questioning whether the buyers will earn enough from AI to justify it. That is a timing gap, not a contradiction.

What business leaders should take from it:

	1.	Fund AI projects with measurable outcomes, not fear of missing out
	2.	Avoid long, rigid commitments on infrastructure and pricing
	3.	Build budgets that work whether AI costs rise or fall
	4.	Understand the financial health of your critical AI vendors
	5.	Measure returns, not usage

The companies that do this will be well positioned whichever signal proves right.

Read the full analysis, "Nvidia's Record Quarter vs Wall Street's AI Doubts: What the AI Spending Boom Means for Business," on my website:

www.ashwinchekavan.com

Foreign investors have put ₹84,291 crore into Indian shares so far this November. In rupees, that's already the biggest month in depository data going back to 2002.

In the 10 months before it, they pulled out ₹2.95 lakh crore.

So is the foreign money coming back?

I went through every month of foreign flows since 2002. The big comebacks keep coming down to 5 things. Here they are, then and now.

[1] Global money gets cheaper

After the US Fed cut rates to near zero in March 2020, foreigners put ₹2.25 lakh crore into Indian shares from May to December.
Today, the Fed is holding at 3.75% to 4%, 2 of its members voted for a hike on 28 October, and futures traders expect a hike on 9 December.

Missing.

[2] India grows faster than the rest

2023, when India was the fastest-growing major economy, brought in ₹1.71 lakh crore, the biggest year in rupees.
Today, GDP grew 7.8% in April to June, and Bank of America puts the rise in Nifty 50 profits for July to September at about 18%.

In place.

[3] Prices have already fallen

The Sensex lost 52% in 2008 and foreigners sold ₹52,987 crore. In 2009 they bought ₹83,424 crore.
Today, after an 11% bounce from its October low, MSCI India trades at about 20 times next year's earnings, below its 5-year average. Other emerging markets are cheaper still.

Partly.

[4] Inflation and the rupee settle down

As the rupee slid to a record low in 2013, foreigners sold ₹23,036 crore from June to August. Once it steadied, they bought ₹52,966 crore in the next 4 months.
Today, inflation was 6.09% in October, the RBI raised rates on 7 October, and the rupee hit a record low near 97 to the dollar in May. It's about 94 now. What's better than 2013 is the current account deficit, at 0.5% of GDP in April to June.

Missing.

[5] A turning point at home

In May 2009, an election result sent the Sensex up 17% in a day, and foreigners bought ₹20,117 crore that month.
This year, the interim trade deal with the US in February brought tariffs down from 50%, and foreigners bought ₹22,615 crore that month. Then the Iran war began on 28 February, and March became the biggest month of foreign selling on record. The formal trade agreement still isn't signed.

Missing.

The big comeback years had several of these at once. 2009 had 3. Today India has 1, and part of another.

November's buying has had help from outside. Brent has fallen from about $118 a barrel on 30 October to about $96, and money has been leaving the AI-heavy markets after their fall.

None of this tells you where the Nifty goes next. What I'm watching is the Fed on 9 December, oil and the rupee.

India's GCC boom is getting difficult to ignore.

I tracked announcements across India over the past month.

Here's what companies are actually doing.

#Hyderabad

• Mars: Opened 60,000 sq ft; targets 1,000 associates.

• SEI : Inaugurated 1,200-workstation facility; currently employs around 800.

• SplashBI I: Opened 20,000 sq ft; plans $100M investment.

• Bank of America: Leased 10.10 lakh sq ft.

• HCA Healthcare: Pre-leased 6.44 lakh sq ft.

#Bengaluru

• RSM: Inaugurated a 154,000 sq ft office.

• Gilead Sciences: Opened a GCC focused on AI and cybersecurity.

• Suffolk Construction : Launched GCC; plans over 200 hires.

• Blackstone : Established GCC within its second India office.

#Pune

• A.P. Moller - Maersk: Opened centre with 2,000-employee capacity.

#Uttar Pradesh

• Havells India Ltd : Proposed ₹879 crore GCC investment.

• LG Soft India : Proposed ₹634 crore GCC investment.

• Ameriprise Financial Services, LLC  Proposed ₹112.84 crore GCC investment.

• MetLife : Proposed ₹84 crore GCC investment.

All four projects received government approval.

Exciting, ambitious, revealing.

But here's what caught my attention.

Some companies are building new capabilities.
Others are expanding their existing footprint.
And some investments are still proposals.

These aren't the same milestones.
The real opportunity goes beyond jobs and office space.

For now, it's about AI, engineering, innovation, and global ownership. Let's see how this keeps evolving 

The next GCC race isn't about space. It's about influence.

How did I end up in the Patriots Front Office?

Wel…over 200 calls during my transition included people in roles like:

Head of HR, Adidas North America

LinkedIn, Head of Veteran Programs

Senior Partners at EY & Deloitte

Executives at JP Morgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo

Executives at TD Garden
(I messed up that one 😭)

Head Security Consultant for the Krafts and Gillette Stadium
(led to paid Red Team gig 👇)

CEOs of $10M+ companies 

Senior Operations Managers at Amazon and FEDEX

Head of HR at Novartis

Change Management Lead at CISCO

and plenty of Project or Program Managers (how I know I didn’t want to do that)

I could go on and on…

But I ended up averaging about 1 call a day during the week for a year (not too difficult)

And asked as many people for calls as I needed to get them scheduled
(you miss 100% of the shots you don’t take)

Some came from events at my kids’ school (not everything was LinkedIn)

And others came from contractors in my organization (no stone unturned)

#quinnsights

3 keys to my success?

1 - put real effort into my profile so they can see what we have in common AND that I will “put in the work”

2 - personalize notes…highlighting something in common and stressing it is for advice figuring out what I want to do next (not a job)

3 - posting regular content so many of them had either seen me before OR could see that I am active (and had more than 30 connections)

It isn’t rocket science 

LinkedIn gives you the ability to find people you have something in common with (#veterans) all over the world 

You just have to ask and be human

Questions?
Anything you would add?

Day 1 of Generative AI in Finance: why this industry is such a strong fit for AI

I started my Generative AI in Finance course today. The first session was about the why behind the technology, and a few examples stood out:
JP Morgan Chase & Co: AI now handles loan document review that used to take lawyers around 360,000 hours a year.

Bank of America: Its assistant Erica has handled over 1.5 billion customer interactions.

Barclays: AI monitors transactions in real time and blocks fraud before it completes.

Paytm: Its AI Soundbox gives merchants business insights in 11 local languages.

ICICI Bank Prudential Life: Its AUSIS platform processes policies in under 60 seconds.

Five problems in finance that AI is well suited to solve:

Document overload: Millions of pages of loans, claims, and contracts to review.

Speed of fraud: Fraud completes in milliseconds, while human review takes hours.

Advice at scale: One advisor can serve 50 to 100 clients, but banks serve millions.

Changing regulation: One missed compliance update can mean heavy fines.

Fast markets: Prices move faster than any person can read, analyze, and act.

Why this matters: The numbers show the scale. KPMG reports that 83% of finance teams use AI for predictive modeling and scenario analysis, and 91% of financial services companies are already using or evaluating AI.

For me, the biggest takeaway is that in finance, AI has to be accurate and explainable, not just impressive.

Over the coming weeks I’ll be building a RAG-based finance advisor, an AI trading agent, and a fraud detection system. I’ll share what I learn along the way.

If you work in fintech or AI, I’d value your perspective: which problem in finance do you think AI will change most in the next few years?

Buffett Dumped Airlines. Berkshire Now Owns $5.4 Billion of Delta.

In 2020, Warren Buffett sold every airline share Berkshire owned. The world had changed for airlines, he said.

This year, under its new CEO, Berkshire built a $5.4 billion stake in Delta.

Greg Abel took over from Buffett in January. Nine months in, here's what's different:

→ Airlines are back: the Delta stake, first bought early this year.
→ Buybacks are back: Berkshire hadn't bought back a single share since May 2024. Abel restarted in March, then spent $9.6 billion in July to September alone. That's four times what it spent on all other stocks that quarter.
→ Homes are in: it nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar.
→ Banks are trimmed: it sold about 6% of its Bank of America shares, a long-time Buffett favourite.

(A buyback is when a company buys its own shares. Each remaining share then owns a bigger slice of the business.)

It's like a new chef at a legendary restaurant bringing back the dish the old chef took off the menu.

What concerns me
→ Airlines and homebuilders are boom-and-bust businesses. Fuel prices and mortgage rates can wipe out profits fast. In October, Delta cut its profit forecast because fuel costs jumped.
→ Many people copy Berkshire's trades from its quarterly filings. But those filings land up to 45 days after the quarter ends. And the picks are no longer Buffett's.

My view
For me, change isn't the problem. Buffett himself chose Abel. But the Berkshire name no longer means "Buffett's picks". I'd judge the new boss on his results, not on the old boss's legend.

Would you still copy Berkshire's trades now that Buffett isn't the one making them?

Not investment advice. Views are my own.

Apple Pay and a dozen other Apple services went down today

#Apple Pay, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Card, Sign In with Apple and Apple Support all reported problems this afternoon. Some iPhone and Mac users were signed out of their Apple accounts and could not sign back in. Others could not activate new devices.

According to Downdetector, Apple Pay reports started rising around 17:40 CET and peaked around 18:15 CET. iCloud reports surged at about the same time.

Apple has now explained the cause. An internal update took several systems offline, and the company told Bloomberg it was not a cyberattack. Apple says many systems are back online and it is working to restore the rest.

The timing is notable. On Monday, an outage that started at Chase also hit Wells Fargo, Bank of America and Zelle®. Last week, Microsoft 365 and Outlook went down, and a communications failure disrupted air traffic across the US.

That is four major disruptions in about a week. In each case, one provider’s failure stopped payments, banking, email or travel for millions of people.

Jio Credit Limited gross AUM grew 154% in a year while parent Jio Financial Services consolidated profit fell 51%. The annual dividend moved from Q2 to Q1. 

At end-September 2026, ₹1.30 lakh crore of Jio Financial Services ₹1.82 lakh crore in assets sat in investments and ₹37,493 crore in loans. 

In Q2 last year, consolidated dividend income was ₹269 crore and Q1 this year had ₹509 crore, including payouts on its Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) shares. Net profit fell to ₹340.44 crore from ₹695.04 crore, 27% below Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd  estimate. 

Jio Financial Services said that, excluding last year’s dividend, consolidated income rose 132% and operating profit before provisions rose 85% to ₹574 crore, while Jio Credit Limited own operating profit before provisions rose 151% to ₹201 crore. 

Finance costs, already inside that ₹574 crore, rose to ₹578 crore from ₹136 crore, and the company says consolidating Reliance Services and Holdings lifts income and operating profit without changing profit after tax. 

Three items sit below operating profit: 

→ Provisions: ₹41 crore, up from ₹13 crore, which the company links to the group’s expansion.
→ Associates and joint ventures: a ₹44 crore loss, against ₹217 crore of income last year.
→ Tax: ₹489 crore before tax became ₹340.44 crore after tax. 

Jio Financial Services reported that Jio Credit Limited own profit after tax for the quarter was ₹120 crore, up 140% year on year. 

Bank of America has agreed to take up to 49.9% of Jio Credit Limited, subject to approvals. Over six months, profit after tax was ₹1,171 crore, and earnings quality matters as much as growth. 

When a business grows fast, but its profit falls, what do you check first?

Sunday Emails, Late Nights & The Meaning of Professionalism.
 
On Tuesday, I asked why we invest so much in teaching freshers' workplace culture, while assuming experienced leaders automatically have it figured out.
 
One blind spot in that assumption is that the rules of "professionalism" have quietly changed.
Early on, we learn two unwritten rules:
Being available = commitment.
Working late = dedication.
 
I remember a quarterly review meeting where a senior leader pointed out it was 7 PM and no one from his team was on the floor, concluding they lacked commitment. Yet it was post-official working hours.
 
Of course, shift-based roles in healthcare, logistics, or customer operations genuinely require extended coverage, and those expectations are clear upfront. That is very different from using late hours as a yardstick for commitment when the role does not demand it.
 
Today, that mindset creates real friction:
- 3 in 4 Gen Z professionals prioritize work-life balance over titles, viewing constant after- hours availability as poor boundaries rather than dedication (Bank of America & Emeritus 2026).
 - 44% of Indian employees report burnout, though the odds drop by 93% when leaders are approachable (O.C. Tanner 2026 Global Culture Report).
 
Take the Sunday 8 PM email. A leader sends a quick update, leaving the receiver stuck: Should I reply now to show commitment, or wait until Monday and look disengaged?
Leadership is not just what you intend. People learn from what you repeatedly model.
 
Professionalism today is not constant availability. It is modeling healthy boundaries so teams thrive (a core focus of The Experience Edge).
 
What is one old rule of “professionalism” you have had to unlearn?

''India leads the world in flexible workspaces. Not the US. Not the UK. India''.

On this week’s Fika Friday at the Office, I sat down over a lemon iced tea in Bengaluru with Amit RamaniRamani, Founder, Chairman & MD of Awfis Space Solutions Limited. 
He built India’s flex category before most of us knew the word.

5 things that stayed with me:

1️⃣ India has the highest flex penetration in the world. About 12% of India’s billion sq ft of office space is flex, growing 20–25% a year. Amit expects the sector to double in five years. In his words, “This is a Zomato moment. The behavior has changed forever.”

2️⃣ Hybrid work is 25 years old. After 9/11, Amit’s team at HOK was designing hybrid, hoteling and work-from-home programs for AmEx and Bank of America. COVID didn’t invent hybrid. It made it mainstream.

3️⃣ GCCs follow a three-step path. Start in co-working at about 50 seats, move to a managed office at about 500, then build your own campus at 2,500+. Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai take about 75% of the growth, and Tier-2 cities like Coimbatore, Kochi and Indore are next.

4️⃣ Design is 20% aesthetics. The rest is how people actually use the space. Widen a corridor from 6 to 12 feet, add a few touchpoints, and you get conversations no office policy can mandate.

5️⃣ Robots will redesign the office. “When the physical AI comes in, as early as 3–4 years from now, the physical workplace will need to adapt.” A robot that works 24 hours and a human who works 8–10 need very different spaces.

And his closing line: “There are two things you can’t choose in life: your parents and the country you’re born in. We are extremely fortunate.”

Thank you, Amit, for a brilliant fika ☕.

A woman in the Nilgiris can now send her child to private school because someone decided to turn her craft skills into a business.

Sunita Suhas and Suhas Ramegowda had spent around 15 years in the corporate world, including leadership roles at companies such as Shell, Bank of America and Accenture.

In 2016, they took a 10,000-km road trip across 14 Indian states. They spent much of the journey in rural India, meeting communities and learning how people lived.

A year later, they left Bengaluru and moved to the Nilgiris, a hill region in Tamil Nadu. Neighbours kept dropping by with bananas, greens and eggs, and soon the couple was part of the community. 

Living there, they realized: many women had skills, but very few opportunities to earn from them.

So, in 2019, they started the Indian Yards Foundation in Ooty to train women from rural and indigenous communities in crafts. Sunita, who often learns new crafts from YouTube, began with five women in their living room. 

They started making quilts and selling them online. Within a year, the business reportedly generated ₹30 lakh in revenue.

When the pandemic hit, they adapted again. Using leftover fabric, they began making three-layered masks after consulting doctors. They also experimented with crochet, embroidery, and macramé.

The team grew from five women to 21.

They became famous when the rag doll she made from leftover fabric, like the ones grandmothers once stitched, became a hit. Within a month, people called it the Indian Barbie, and they set aside almost everything else. 

In 2021, they incorporated their craft startup and by 2023 launched their brand, The Good Doll. Rainmatter by Zerodha became their first investor. By 2025, they had introduced Nilah, an Indian doll inspired by the Nilgiris and the Neelakurinji flowers that bloom once every 12 years.

📌Today, more than 100 women make 4,000 to 5,000 dolls a month, and for many it is their first formal job. 
📌More than half now add significantly to their household income, and some earn more than their husbands. 
📌For many, it has meant a scooter, a new home, a private school for their children, and better food at home. 

Somewhere along the way, a small craft project became a source of income, confidence, and greater independence for women and their families in Nilgiris.

I think that's one of the most meaningful things a business can do: create opportunities that allow people to see a different future for themselves and their families.

Have you come across any other Indian brands creating livelihoods through traditional skills?
